title: MLB strikes out in effort to trademark ‘Play Ball’ phrase for use on clothing
content:
The United States Patent and Trademark Office has refused to play ball with Major League Baseball’s effort to trademark one of sports’ most well-known phrases.

In a final ruling brief issued Saturday, the agency rejected MLB’s effort to trademark “Play Ball” for use on clothing. MLB sought to secure sweeping ownership of the colloquialism in all clothing contexts, regardless of styling and font. While the USPTO acknowledged the phrase’s baseball roots, officials found its modern use goes beyond sports and is part of common parlance.

That common use runs counter to the purpose of a trademark, which exists to prevent the public from misinterpreting a phrase or term as an indication that a specific entity is selling a certain product.

The USPTO ruled that “Play Ball” does not carry an exclusive association with MLB, pointing to its use as a general reference to cooperation or an indication to start something. As such, the agency found, the expression is informational rather than identifiable with MLB itself.

“Registration is refused because the applied-for mark is a slogan or term that does not function as a trademark or service mark to indicate the source of applicant’s goods and/or services and to identify and distinguish them from others,” the ruling said.

“… Because consumers are accustomed to seeing this term or expression commonly used in everyday speech by many different sources, they would not perceive it as a mark identifying the source of applicant’s goods and/or services but rather as only conveying an informational message.”

MLB applied for the “Play Ball” trademark in 2022. It has three months to appeal for reconsideration. The league does own a trademark on the term “Play Ball Park” for use in entertainment contexts, as well as a clothing trademark on “Take Me Out to the Ballgame.”

An attorney representing MLB’s claim was not available for comment. The USPTO did not respond to a request for comment.

Dozens of companies have previously applied for trademarks on other forms of the phrase with mixed results.

For instance, one trademark approved in 1996 protects the use of “Play Ball!” in reference to an “absorbent granular material for drying the surface of playgrounds and ball fields.” Recent applications to protect phrases such as “Let’s Play Ball,” “Don’t Cry, Play Ball” and “Shut Up & Play Ball” have failed or been abandoned.
